tagline: Three horns and a week of playful choices.
bigIdea: One dinosaur, many ways to notice.

dinosaur.name: Triceratops
dinosaur.feature: Triceratops had three horns and a frill.

letter.hint: Say /t/, not the letter name. Clip /t/ without adding “uh.”

number.focus: Choose the food; give four from a pile of eight.
number.parentTip: Serve four from a pile of eight. Keep extras within reach; let {{them}} decide when to stop. Five only if {{they}} want{{s}} more.

books.title: How Do Dinosaurs Say Good Night?
books.author: Jane Yolen; art: Mark Teague

songs: We Are the Dinosaurs — Laurie Berkner. March or sway.
Five Enormous Dinosaurs — traditional. Stomp and count a few.
Twinkle Twinkle Little Star — traditional. Hear /t/ in “twinkle.”
materials: 8 magnet tiles (4 each of 2 colors), cloth
parentNote: Stay and play for 2–10 minutes. Choose one route; stop on pushback. Books and songs are choices, not a checklist.

days.title: Hello, Triceratops!
days.invitation: Want to color Triceratops, or roll a dough loop for it?
days.decision: Which spoken word starts with /t/: sock or towel?
days.harder: If that sound game is easy, try a fresh spoken pair: sun or tap.
days.what: Want to color Triceratops, or roll a dough loop for it? Share the dinosaur strip as you play. Let {{them}} color or join the ends of a dough snake. A free crayon circle on scrap is welcome too. For a sound turn, say “sock” and “towel” naturally; ask which starts with /t/. If the words or game are new, show one together first. Point to T and model /t/; an echo is welcome. If {{they}} want{{s}} a repeat, reverse the spoken word order.
days.why: A familiar spoken word gives the new sound somewhere to belong.

days.needs: Page, card, crayons, scrap paper, playdough, washable mat; parent present.

days.title: Dinner for Triceratops
days.invitation: Want to squash a leafy dinner, or build Triceratops a pen?
days.decision: Which food belongs to Triceratops, and when are four leaves enough?
days.harder: Clear the plate, return all eight leaves, and invite five if four was easy.
days.what: Want to squash a leafy dinner, or build Triceratops a pen? Share that Triceratops ate plants. Make eight pretend dough leaves together. If {{they}} build{{s}} the pen first, make the eight leaves while {{they}} build{{s}}. Later, offer the leaf/meat pictures: which is its food? Put all eight leaves together off the plate and ask for four on it. Let {{them}} decide when to stop; no numeral reading needed.
days.why: An empty plate leaves the stopping decision to {{them}}.

days.title: Who ate something different?
days.invitation: Want to tell a dinosaur dinner story, or hide a picture after the story?
days.decision: Which dinosaur ate meat instead of plants?
days.harder: Invite the hidden dinosaur’s name and food before uncovering it.
days.exitCheck: Which dinosaur did {{they}} pick, and what did {{they}} say about its food?
days.what: Want to tell a dinosaur dinner story, or hide a picture after the story? First tell their dinner story: Stegosaurus, Triceratops and Ankylosaurus ate plants; T. rex ate meat. Put this card aside and play with the pictures awhile. Later, shuffle and ask who ate meat. If {{they}} pick{{s}} another difference, listen to {{their}} reason, then return to the food question. For hiding, name the four together; cover one while {{they}} look{{s}} away and invite {{them}} to guess.
days.why: Diet is something to learn and remember; a silhouette alone cannot tell it.

days.title: What comes next?
days.invitation: Want to build a tile trail, or choose the next picture?
days.decision: Which picture continues the Stegosaurus–Triceratops pattern?
days.harder: After {{their}} first tile choice, offer one more place, with both colors available again.
days.exitCheck: What did {{they}} choose to come next?
days.what: Want to build a tile trail, or choose the next picture? Show red–blue–red–blue and add red together. Take it all apart. Then lay blue–red–blue–red; offer one tile of each color for the next place. Or name the printed row together, leaving its blank for {{name}}. Keep both picture choices available; {{they}} can point or park a card below the blank. One route is enough.
days.why: The objects change, but the repeating relationship stays the same.
days.cardBlurb: Four red and four blue magnet tiles (any two colors work). Cut the two picture choices; keep the row whole. Want to build a tile trail, or choose the next picture? Show red–blue–red–blue and add red together. Take it all apart. Then lay blue–red–blue–red; offer one tile of each color for the next place. Or name the printed row together, leaving its blank for {{name}}. Keep both picture choices available; {{they}} can point or park a card below the blank. One route is enough. Stop on pushback.
days.needs: Page, card, scissors, eight magnet tiles (four each of two colors); parent present.

days.title: A book for Triceratops
days.invitation: Want to turn the pages while I read, or make a dough resting place first?
days.decision: Which picture word starts with /t/: towel or sock?
days.harder: Cover the pictures and invite the sound for T, if {{they}} want{{s}} another turn.
days.exitCheck: Did {{they}} make a crayon circle with the ends meeting?
days.what: Want to turn the pages while I read, or make a dough resting place first? Read the captions as {{they}} turn{{s}} pages; {{they}} {{is}} not expected to read them. Talk about the dinosaur eating plants. Name “towel” and “sock” naturally before asking which starts with /t/. Show T and model the sound. On the last page, {{they}} can join a dough snake into a resting loop, or make {{their}} own crayon circle on scrap. No need to do every part. If {{they}} want{{s}} a repeat, reverse the spoken word order.
days.why: Familiar sounds return in a short book {{they}} can hold and help tell.
